plays.why_it_works: Ira's grudge against Chuck is fresher and more personal than his grudge against Axe, and Axe meets his real needs, money and his relationship. Having Ira accuse Chuck, instead of simply staying quiet, turns a hostile witness into a weapon against the prosecutor who set Axe up.
plays.outcome: Ira tells the prosecutors that Chuck induced the scheme and that Chuck's trust money was involved. The lead prosecutor shuts him down, but Bryan Connerty picks up the thread and goes after Chuck's father.
plays.counter: The prosecutors should have locked in Ira's testimony early. Chuck should have repaired the friendship with Ira instead of paying him off cheaply and leaving the grievance open for Axe to buy.
plays.principle: Win over the other side's witness by giving him a better enemy and a better deal.
plays.in_practice: When a disgruntled former client is lining up to criticize you, find out what they actually need (money back, an apology, a way to save face) and whom they blame most. Meeting that need honestly can turn a critic into an advocate.

quote.text: I'm willing to pay you 30 million to tell the truth.
quote.speaker: Bobby Axelrod

plays.title: Recruit the Betrayed Ally
plays.strategist: Mike Ross, Louis Litt and Robert Zane
plays.target: Stanley Gordon, Eric Kaldor and Ellen Rand
plays.context: Former partners led by Stanley Gordon are suing the firm. If it rehires them, they will vote to merge it into Rand Kaldor Zane; if it fights, it may lose the suit and go bankrupt. Robert Zane, the rival managing partner who has always refused to join forces with Harvey Specter's firm, has just learned that his own partners of 26 years, Eric Kaldor and Ellen Rand, went behind his back.
plays.play: Mike Ross proposes rehiring Gordon's group but also bringing in Zane with about twenty loyal lawyers, so the firm keeps control of the vote. Louis Litt objects that Zane has always said no; Mike points out that they have never asked him right after his own partners cut his legs out. Zane resists and says he will think about it. The next morning, while Louis is signing Gordon's agreement, Zane walks in and announces that Gordon's clients are joining a new merged firm, set up that morning before Gordon could block it. He did not tell Louis in advance in case Louis gave it away, and he insists his name goes first.
plays.why_it_works: The betrayal that hurt Zane is what made him available: his own firm was no longer safe for him. Moving before anyone could react left Gordon no time to counter, and keeping it from Louis meant nothing leaked.
plays.outcome: The firm becomes Zane Specter Litt, the takeover plot fails and Gordon is beaten. Harvey returns to a firm with a new name partner he did not pick.
plays.counter: Rand and Kaldor forgot that betraying Zane gave him a motive to join the other side. Before you betray a powerful partner, ask where he will go.
plays.principle: The best time to recruit someone is right after their own side has betrayed them.
plays.in_practice: When a senior person at a partner or competitor falls out with their own organization, that is the moment they will consider options they have always rejected. Approach them quickly and respectfully.

quote.text: Have we ever asked him right after Rand and Kaldor cut his legs out?
quote.speaker: Mike Ross

plays.title: Split the Witness From the Company
plays.target: Frank DiBiase of Logan Tech
plays.context: Rosalie Williams, returning to law, represents graduates of a for-profit college, Logan Tech, who were promised jobs that never came. The college denies making the promises. Samantha Wheeler, a name partner at the firm, books the deposition of the admissions executive Frank DiBiase in her own office to intimidate him.
plays.play: They establish that half of DiBiase's pay is tied to loan originations, so it made no difference to him whether students got jobs. Samantha tells him that once they prove he was paid to say whatever it took, they can come after him personally. When Logan Tech's lawyer says the company will indemnify him, Samantha asks whom that lawyer is really looking out for, predicts the company will hang him out to dry, and offers to waive his personal liability now, for this one chance only.
plays.why_it_works: A witness and the company paying his lawyer have different interests. Exposing his personal liability, casting doubt on the company's loyalty and offering a one-time escape turns him into an ally.
plays.outcome: DiBiase admits he lied about the numbers and that the board told him to. Logan Tech is forced onto the defensive, claiming it will go bankrupt at anything above $15,000 per plaintiff.
plays.counter: Logan Tech should have given DiBiase independent counsel, so there was no conflict to exploit.
plays.principle: Find the gap between a person's interests and their organization's, and offer them a way out through it.
plays.in_practice: In a negotiation with an organization, understand what the individual across the table personally risks and gains. A proposal that protects them often moves faster than one aimed only at the company.

quote.text: Who do you think she's looking out for, Frank? You or Logan Tech?
quote.speaker: Samantha Wheeler

plays.title: Siggy's Hedge
plays.target: Rollo, Ragnar and Lagertha, then King Horik
plays.context: Siggy is the wife of Earl Haraldson, the ruler of Kattegat, and her power depends entirely on him. As his contest with Ragnar Lothbrok grows she faces ruin if the wrong side wins, and after it she is a widow with a daughter and no position.
plays.play: While still the Earl's wife she secretly warns Rollo to leave, then sends word to Ragnar that Rollo is being tortured to lure him, putting Ragnar in her debt (S01E05). After Haraldson's death she accepts Rollo's protection and asks Lagertha, Ragnar's wife, to let her serve in her household, while feeding Rollo's resentment of his brother (S01E06 to S01E08). In Season 2 she opens a second line: she offers King Horik, Ragnar's senior ally and rival, the knowledge of Ragnar's weaknesses, becomes his lover and passes him gossip. She tells Rollo that if the allies fall out, he should be able to choose between them. When Horik finally demands the promised weakness she names Ragnar's children, and Horik asks her to kill the boys in return for making her a queen. When his attack comes, she leads them to safety instead (S02E10).
plays.why_it_works: Siggy keeps a quiet line to every likely winner before the contest is decided, so she has credit whichever way power moves, and gives each patron just enough to stay engaged. At the decisive moment she chooses the side she is actually bound to, which is what makes a hedge worth having.
plays.outcome: She survives her husband's fall, keeps her daughter under Lagertha's protection, becomes Rollo's partner, and wins Horik's trust so fully that he reveals his plan, which lets her save Ragnar's sons.
plays.counter: Horik noticed that she never delivered on her promise and should have treated an informant who gives nothing concrete as a possible double agent. Ragnar and Lagertha accepted her service without seeing that she was also working on Rollo.
plays.principle: Keep a door open to every power in the room, and know before the crisis which one you will walk through.
plays.in_practice: In a client organization facing a leadership change, build real relationships with the likely successors early and be useful across factions. Your value to all of them depends on it being clear where your core loyalty lies when a decision is forced.

quote.text: Right now they are allies... long may they remain so... but in the event that they should fall out, you should be able to choose between them.
quote.speaker: Siggy

plays.title: Whispering in Both Ears
plays.target: Vice President Jim Matthews and President Garrett Walker
plays.context: Frank Underwood, the House Majority Whip, groomed Congressman Peter Russo to run for governor of Pennsylvania and then engineered his collapse. With Russo gone seven weeks before the election, Frank's real aim comes into view: Vice President Jim Matthews, a former Pennsylvania governor, should resign and run, opening the vice presidency for Frank. Neither Matthews nor President Garrett Walker would propose it, since leaving looks like demotion and pushing out a vice president looks like weakness.
plays.play: Frank tells Matthews he knows no one with the name recognition to start from scratch, then says there is one person: him. When Matthews says Walker needs him in 2016, Frank reluctantly reports that Walker called him a pain in the ass, and adds that Russo had noticed how much Matthews missed being governor. He asks Matthews to keep the talk to himself and promises not to mention it to Walker. He then tells Walker the idea is entirely his own, relays that Matthews complained Walker lacks leadership, and proposes a face-saving structure: a joint statement that Matthews will resign only if he wins, so neither man looks disloyal.
plays.why_it_works: Each man hears that the other already disrespects him, which makes parting look attractive and mutual. The joint statement removes the main objection, the appearance of disloyalty or weakness, and by keeping each conversation secret Frank stops them comparing notes. Attributing observations to the now-silent Russo makes them impossible to check.
plays.outcome: Walker agrees and Matthews signs on, praising Frank's bold move. The vice presidency will be vacant as soon as Matthews wins.
plays.counter: Walker and Matthews could have spoken directly before deciding; one honest conversation would have exposed that each was hearing the other's grievances from the same man.
plays.principle: To part two allies, let each believe it was the other's wish, and give both a face-saving way out.
plays.in_practice: The ethical version is designing a win-win exit: when a partnership has run its course, propose a transition both sides can announce as mutual. Defensively, if one person is carrying messages between you and someone else, check with the source directly.

quote.text: Well, the exact phrase he used was "Pain in the ass."
quote.speaker: Frank Underwood

plays.title: Talking Past the Lawyer
plays.target: The 200 Apple Creek plaintiffs and Harvey Specter
plays.context: Harvey Specter represents some 200 residents of Apple Creek, New York, in a class action over cancer clusters. A class action is only as strong as its unity: if enough plaintiffs take a quick payout, the case collapses. Travis Tanner, the opposing lawyer and Harvey's old rival, is not allowed to contact represented plaintiffs directly.
plays.play: A man claiming to be from Harvey's firm visits one plaintiff, says an offer is coming and warns that the other side has dirt on everyone, naming one plaintiff's arrest for public drunkenness and another's college shoplifting. Tanner has the plaintiffs invited to the Waldorf to hear a settlement offer. When Harvey arrives, Tanner says he cannot talk to the clients, but he can talk to Harvey. He then announces $25,000 a plaintiff loudly enough for the whole room to hear, hands out his number, and apologizes for raising his voice.
plays.why_it_works: Fear works on the most vulnerable members of a group, and a concrete, quick payout gives them an easy way out. Using a proxy and 'talking to the lawyer' keeps Tanner technically inside the rules while his message reaches every plaintiff.
plays.outcome: Ninety-five plaintiffs call Tanner about the offer and the case is close to collapse. Harvey knows the proxy will never be traced back to Tanner.
plays.counter: Tell the members of a coalition in advance what attacks are coming, and give the weakest members a better alternative than the payout, which is what Harvey then does.
plays.principle: To break a coalition, frighten its weakest members and hand them an easy exit.
plays.in_practice: In a group deal, joint venture or partnership, expect a competitor to pick off the most anxious member with a quick offer. Look after your weakest links before anyone else reaches them.

quote.text: I know I can't talk to your clients directly. But thank God you're here, Harv. Because what I can do is I can talk to you.
quote.speaker: Travis Tanner

plays.title: Burn the Hedger
plays.strategist: Frank Underwood (via Seth Grayson), exploiting Remy Danton's hedge
plays.target: Raymond Tusk and Remy Danton
plays.context: Raymond Tusk, a billionaire and President Walker's closest adviser, is at war with Vice President Frank Underwood. Remy Danton, Tusk's lobbyist and chief operator, has been put on paid leave because of an investigation into Chinese money and sees his career ending.
plays.play: Remy meets Frank in a church and offers limited neutrality: he will keep fighting Frank, but only enough to hurt, never enough to finish him, in return for a future after his firm. He says he is backing whoever wins and leaves behind the watch Frank once gave him as a sign of good faith. Frank turns the hedge into a weapon. He sends Seth Grayson, his press secretary, who once spied on Frank for Tusk's side before switching, to see Tusk. Seth doubts Tusk will even talk to him; Frank says that is exactly why he will, since a turncoat who comes back looks like he has something to sell. Seth tells Tusk about the church. Tusk summons Remy to a darkened penthouse with Seth present, makes him admit the meeting, brushes aside his claim that he was feeding Frank false confidence, and throws him out.
plays.why_it_works: A hedge is valuable only while it stays secret, and Remy made his with the one man who gained most from exposing it. The information was true, so no denial could hold, and it came from a known turncoat, which made it look like leaked intelligence instead of a plant.
plays.outcome: Tusk loses his most capable operator on the eve of his testimony and grows more isolated. Remy, left with nothing, is soon recruited to the impeachment effort by Jackie Sharp.
plays.counter: Remy should have told Tusk about the meeting himself before anyone else could. Tusk could have asked why the news was reaching him now, and who gained from the split.
plays.principle: Expose a hedger to his master and you remove two enemies at once.
plays.in_practice: If you are exploring a new partnership while in an existing one, tell your current partner first, or assume a competitor will. When damaging news about an ally reaches you, ask who benefits from your believing it.

quote.text: I don't blame you for wanting to keep your options open. But clearly you have bought the wrong insurance policy.
quote.speaker: Raymond Tusk

plays.title: The Conscience Clause
plays.strategist: Claire Underwood (with Remy Danton setting the price)
plays.target: Frank Underwood and his watershed bill
plays.context: Claire Underwood, Frank's wife and partner, runs a clean water charity. $200,000 of its water filters are stuck in customs in South Sudan. The State Department cannot help, and Frank refuses to ask Remy Danton, the lobbyist for the gas company Sancorp, whose contacts could free them, because Remy is fighting Frank's watershed bill. Claire has already sacrificed staff and donors for Frank's plans and feels her goals always come second. Remy tells her Sancorp will help, at a price: kill the bill.
plays.play: Claire keeps her charity publicly behind the bill but takes Remy's deal. When Frank sends her to shore up two wavering congressmen, she tells them privately that she shares their doubts, that Frank would never fault them for voting their conscience, and that if the bill fails it is not the end of the world. She uses Frank's own principle as her cover. Then she calls Frank and reports both as definite yeses, so the whip counts them until the vote closes.
plays.why_it_works: She is the one person Frank trusts completely, so he sends her unsupervised into the decisive meeting. Quoting his own rule makes the permission to defect sound authorized, and the false report blinds him until it is too late to recover.
plays.outcome: The bill is defeated on the floor and Claire gets her filters. Frank frightens the two congressmen into saying who told them to vote no, then confronts Claire; the fight exposes how each has been using the other, and she leaves for New York.
plays.counter: Frank ignored the warning sign of an unmet need at home: Claire had asked for help and been refused, which made her available to a rival's offer. He also accepted a report of definite votes without confirming them himself.
plays.principle: An ally whose needs you keep refusing is an ally your rival can buy.
plays.in_practice: Partners and key staff who feel their goals always come second become open to competitors' offers. Ask regularly what your closest people need, and verify critical commitments yourself instead of relying on a secondhand 'it's done'.

quote.text: if the bill fails, it's not the end of the world. We can always sponsor new legislation.
quote.speaker: Claire Underwood

plays.title: The Jealous King
plays.target: Ragnar Lothbrok (and Jarl Borg)
plays.context: King Horik of Denmark is the senior partner in an alliance with Ragnar Lothbrok, now Earl of Kattegat, but Ragnar is the leader men follow. Horik also nurses old grudges against Jarl Borg, the third partner in their raid on England.
plays.play: Horik starts by cutting Borg out of the raid (S02E02). When Ragnar protests that they had an agreement, Horik points out that Ragnar will not take his own brother because he does not trust him, and says it is the same for him with Borg; then he makes Ragnar deliver the news. With the fleet away, the spurned Borg seizes Kattegat (S02E03). Next Horik works on Ragnar's circle: he takes Siggy as lover and informant, tells Lagertha that she and he are at least Ragnar's equal, and tells the boat builder Floki he is worth ten earls (S02E06, S02E08). He rebukes Ragnar in public for sending an envoy to King Ecbert without consulting him. When Ecbert sends envoys under a guarantee of safe passage, Horik's men kill all but Ecbert's son, and Horik forbids Ragnar from talking alone, then leads the charge that loses the battle (S02E09).
plays.why_it_works: Each move is locally clever: borrowing Ragnar's own standard makes objection look inconsistent, and courting Ragnar's people with the recognition Ragnar neglects is a sound way to build a bloc. Together they fail, because Horik treats his partners as rivals to be diminished, so every win for his pride costs the alliance a capability.
plays.outcome: Borg's revenge costs Ragnar his home, the parley is wrecked, and the allies are beaten in Wessex and forced to negotiate from weakness. The people Horik courted turn out to be loyal to Ragnar when Horik finally moves against him (S02E10).
plays.counter: Ragnar's counter is patience: he concedes points of process 'because he is the king', lets Horik's leadership fail on its own, and keeps his people's real loyalty. He should also have agreed with Horik before landing what the allies wanted, land or revenge, since partners with different goals will sabotage each other at the table.
plays.principle: An ally who competes with you for rank will spend the alliance's strength to win.
plays.in_practice: In a joint venture, agree the goal and who speaks before you meet the client, and settle questions of status in private. Before you drop a partner from a bid, ask what they can do to you while your attention is elsewhere.

quote.text: Because you don't trust him enough. It is the same for me with Jarl Borg.
quote.speaker: King Horik
